Record Q2 2024 results - revenue +23% to $402M, gross margin 52%, adjusted EBITDA ~$100M - but the dominant narrative was a sharply slowing energy category and resulting share volatility.
Celsius contributed 47% of all category growth and grew ~10x the category rate; unit volume +30.6% while the category's Q2 unit volume was flat.

Headwinds: macro pressure on consumer purchasing, a stagnating-then-softening energy category (one large convenience chain SSS down >4%), intensifying competition (notably Red Bull launches), delayed shelf resets/promotions, ~$20-25M distributor inventory timing drag, and a $7.9M legal charge in G&A.
Large shelf-space gains during seasonal resets: average SKUs per store +>35% (+43% convenience) vs the Dec 2023 reset.
Non-tracked channels were a major tailwind: Club +30% to $88M, Amazon +41% to $39.9M; Celsius recaptured #1 Amazon energy share (22.1%) post-Prime Day.
Sequential MULOC share contracted (11% to ~10.5% area) despite growth leadership; management attributed it to competitors' large dollar base and recent launches, but flagged it as a real watch item.
Management explicitly declined to guide on when share would stabilize/re-align with sales: 'we're not going to provide forward-looking guidance on that.'
Switched tracked-channel reference to Circana's MULO Plus geography (12.04% with convenience) to better capture online and club retailers.
The full-sugar energy subset has stagnated; the growth fight has moved to sugar-free, now ~50% of the category; Celsius is the #2 sugar-free brand and is driving the entire category's growth.

Back-half outlook constructive but explicitly cautious: conservative gross margin target of high 40s-to-50%, Q3 S&M spend likely above the 20-23% range, aggressive investment in field sales (+>250% over 12 months), promotions and the Pepsi added-incentive program (fully ramped in H2).

2025 catalysts: room for further pricing (offsetting aluminum/freight inflation), a strong 2025 innovation pipeline (on-the-go powders, 'beyond the can' packaging), international launches (Australia, New Zealand, France on track for later 2024), and 'interesting concepts' for Q1 2025.
International growth strong: revenue +30% in Q2; Canada exceeding expectations, UK/Ireland launched in Q2.
Executive change-in-control agreements & July share trends
What is the purpose of the new Aug 1 employment agreements with change-in-control amendments, and what is being seen in July share trends?

Fieldly: the compensation committee standardized the executive team's change-of-control terms. Langhans: largely administrative - bringing newer executives (CCO, CSCO, CMO, CLO) up to par with John's and Jarrod's existing severance/change-of-control packages as the company expands globally. On July, share moved from 11 to 10 amid heavy competition and consumer challenges; weekly reads are noisy; Celsius still drives 47% of category growth and grows >10x category, but July showed 'further softness within the category.' Observers expect a Q4 recovery but management must be cautious.
Why is Celsius growth meaningfully ahead of the category (~15% vs ~1% over six weeks) yet market share has contracted ~20bps sequentially?

Fieldly: attributed to competitor scale and recent launches - particularly Red Bull's strong launches and recent share gains. Because competitors have such a large dollar base, even with Celsius growing 10x the category, a competitor's 1-1.5 share points of growth on a large base moves the relative share figures.

Will share stabilize/improve, is data showing consumers switching from Celsius to other brands, when does share/sales re-align, and how is pricing being approached given competitor moves and aluminum cost pressure?

Fieldly: watches 1-, 4-, 12-week data; new competitor innovation gets trial but loyal consumers return; confidence from the Amazon-vs-tracked share gap and 15-share markets. Declined a stabilization timeline ('we're not going to provide forward-looking guidance'). Sugar-free now 50% of the category. On pricing: two top competitors have taken pricing; Celsius will maintain its premium position but be cautious given price-sensitive consumers; promotional pricing strategy/architecture is key; increasing Q3 retail marketing investments.
Michael Lavery (Piper Sandler) / Jonathan Keypour (Bank of America)

Is the shift toward Amazon accelerating as C-store is pressured, was Amazon strength Prime-Day-related, what was the actual Q2 Pepsi inventory drag, will a ~$20M drag recur in Q3/Q4, and why did velocity keep declining sequentially after resets?

Fieldly: Amazon and club (larger packs, better per-can value) performed well; convenience declined as a percent of category sales, indicating consumers expanding across channels. Langhans: the $20-30M DOH headwind landed at the low end (~20-25%); the distributor manages its own inventory so 'we'll have to see where they end up'; on velocity, cited timing/sequencing and reset delays that also delayed promotions; the company deliberately held promotions until shelf space was secured to protect ROI; strong Q3/Q4 promotional calendar expected to turn velocities around.
Back-half velocity resilience, category slowdown & innovation contribution
Does the deeper Q3/Q4 program pipeline imply more resilient back-half velocities/share, why is the category slowing now, and have newer flavors been as incremental as expected?

Fieldly: back-half resilience is category-dependent - the category was down on a recent weekly read; the priority is getting the category back to growth. On the slowdown: in total LRB, juices/coffee/tea remained pressured while sports drinks/water/CSDs grew; energy was up only ~2% on a 4-week read to July 14; cited interest-rate pressure and consumers 'taking a pause' but reaffirmed massive upside. On innovation: a 'total portfolio play' (new flavors Sparkling Watermelon Lemonade, Kiwi Strawberry, Cherry Cola, plus Essentials 16oz) drives growth across the portfolio rather than any single flavor.
Pepsi inventory clarification & future shelf space / innovation
Should another Q3 Pepsi inventory headwind be expected, and how confident is management that retailers will give incremental space for the 2025 innovation pipeline?

Langhans: the Q2 DOH impact landed near the low end of $20-30M; 'time will tell' on Q3 - cannot predict the partner's actions; if the distributor's system is fully optimized the company is in good shape but there is still some flexibility to further optimize. Fieldly: the key is continuing to outpace category growth, strengthening the retailer selling story (#1, incremental, driving sugar-free growth); a lot of great 2025 innovation planned; initial 2025 retailer discussions 'fairly positive'; on-the-go powders and 'beyond the can' packaging are additional opportunities.
